subject: Computer Networking
title: PGP and End-to-End Encryption
description: A micro-lesson that makes PGP and End-to-End Encryption usable.

hook.text: TLS encrypts the pipe. PGP encrypts the message itself. Only the intended recipient can decrypt it.

buildup.text: PGP uses a key pair. You encrypt with the recipient's public key. They decrypt with their private key.

discovery.text: No server in the middle can read it. Not Gmail, not your ISP, not the government. True end-to-end.

twist.text: PGP is notoriously hard to use. Key management, trust models, and UX have limited adoption for decades.

climax.text: ProtonMail and Tutanota bake encryption into the UI. Users get PGP-level security without the complexity.

punchline.text: PGP means only you and the recipient can read it. True privacy.

quiz.question: What makes PGP different from TLS for email?
options: PGP encrypts the message itself, not just the connection

details.summary: PGP encrypts email so only the intended recipient can read it, even if servers are compromised. It uses public-key cryptography where the sender encrypts with the recipient's public key and only their private key can decrypt.
details.whyItMatters: PGP provides true end-to-end email privacy where no server, ISP, or government can read the content. Its low adoption shows the trade-off between security and usability.
takeaways: PGP encrypts email end-to-end using public-key cryptography
Only the recipient's private key can decrypt the message
Adoption remains low because of complexity and poor usability

faq.question: Why hasn't PGP been widely adopted despite decades of availability?
faq.answer: PGP requires exchanging public keys, managing keyrings, and using specialized software. The user experience is poor compared to regular email. Key management is confusing for non-technical users. Most people sacrifice privacy for convenience and rely on TLS instead.

faq.question: Are there easier alternatives to PGP for encrypted email?
faq.answer: ProtonMail and Tutanota provide end-to-end encryption with simple interfaces. S/MIME is built into many email clients. However, both sender and recipient must use the same system. For truly universal encrypted email, no easy solution exists because email was not designed for it.
